entities.name: Virius Nicomachus Flavianus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Virius Nicomachus Flavianus (died 394 CE) was a towering figure among the late Roman pagan aristocracy, a distinguished politician, scholar, and religious traditionalist whose career culminated in the last major attempt to restore the ancient Roman gods against the ascendant Christian Empire. A scion of the influential Nicomachi family, his life intersected with the profound religious and political transformations of the late 4th century, positioning him as a vocal champion of paganism alongside his friend Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, and ultimately leading him to support the usurper Eugenius against the Christian emperor Theodosius I.

Flavianus held numerous high offices, including *vicarius Asiae* and, most notably, three terms as *praefectus praetorio Italiae, Illyrici et Africae* (390, 392–394 CE), a position of immense administrative power. Beyond his political acumen, he was a prolific scholar. He composed a lost historical work, the *Annales*, and undertook a critical recension of Livy's monumental *Ab Urbe Condita*, a project vital for the transmission of this classical text. His fervent commitment to traditional Roman religion manifested in his efforts to revive pagan cults and rituals, including his initiation into various mystery religions, making him a central figure in the pagan senatorial resistance.

The defeat and death of Flavianus at the Battle of the Frigidus on September 6, 394 CE, alongside Eugenius, represented a watershed moment. This military catastrophe definitively crushed the last significant political and military challenge to imperial Christianity in the West, ushering in an era of undisputed Christian dominance. While his political and religious cause failed, his scholarly endeavors, particularly the Livy recension, proved enduring, ensuring the survival of crucial classical literature through the tumultuous transition to the Middle Ages. His son, Nicomachus Flavianus the Younger, continued the family's literary patronage.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Flavianus's life and death at the Battle of the Frigidus represented the final, dramatic clash between traditional Roman paganism and the ascendant Christian Empire, definitively ending the political viability of paganism in the West. His scholarly efforts also played a key role in preserving classical Latin literature for future generations.
